sections.h2: Brandenburg offices for your tax bill
sections.html:
Nearly everything happens in two suites at 516 Hillcrest Drive. The assessor, formally the Property Valuation Administration (PVA), is in Suite 3 and takes calls at (270) 422-2178 on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Sheriff's Office is in Suite 14, where payments are accepted, at (270) 422-4937.

One office sets value and the other collects. Bring exemption and value questions to Suite 3, and take the bill itself to Suite 14. The County Clerk gets involved only after April 15, once unpaid bills have been transferred.

Pay the Sheriff. Bills usually go out in the fall, and when mail runs late the Sheriff's office posts an online lookup so owners can check what they owe while the paper bill catches up. The dates below follow KRS 134.015, but the law allows a different schedule when mailing is delayed, so ask the Sheriff which dates apply to your bill.

Meade County payment schedule
When you payEffect on the bill
By November 12 percent discount
Through New Year's EveNo discount, no penalty
January5 percent added
After January10 percent added

Collection ends April 15, and the counter closes at 4:30 that afternoon. Personal checks are refused for the last two weeks of each collection season, so late payers need cash, a card, a money order or a cashier's check. The office calls this a yearly custom, and personal checks are taken again earlier in the season.

sections.h2: What a typical Meade County house owes
sections.html:
The typical owned home is valued at $207,900. The state's 2025 rate is 10.6 cents on each $100, and the county, the school district and special districts add their own levies. Monthly ownership costs run $1,344 with a mortgage and $462 without. Rent is typically $1,026 and household income $74,355.

The county has grown steadily. Its head count rose from 9,422 in 1950 to 18,938 in 1960 and reached 30,003 in 2020. The July 2025 estimate of 30,699 is 2.3 percent above that. Builders pulled 165 permits in 2025, so new houses compete with resale listings.

Owners occupy 74.1 percent of homes. The 2020 census counted 11,943 housing units, 7.5 percent of them vacant, and 27.2 percent of occupied homes were rented. A seller with a tenant in place should settle showing access with the tenant before listing.

Kentucky gives homeowners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, a $49,100 cut in assessed value for 2025 and 2026. It applies before the rates, so it lowers every levy on the bill.

The PVA sets a spring deadline each year for applications to make the November bill. Someone turning 65 soon should call the office to learn the current date. Early filing helps the taxing districts plan. For age, the office accepts a birth certificate, driver's license or passport. A disability claim rests on a total-disability finding and is renewed every year, except for owners with a service-connected disability and anyone with a permanent determination from Social Security or state retirement.

Begin with a PVA conference, where staff show how your value was built. After that, the state calendar governs:

  • Roll viewing lasts 13 days, beginning the first Monday in May.
  • Lodge the appeal at the County Clerk's office before closing on the next business day.
  • Gather land and building records: insurance, construction costs and comparable sale listings.
  • Attend the local board of assessment appeals, which convenes roughly a month after viewing for up to five days.

You may record the hearing. If the board's number ends up above your claim after bills have gone out, a supplemental bill covers the gap.

A sale doesn't wipe the debt out. A bill still open at the April 15 cutoff becomes a certificate in the Clerk's hands, a lien is filed, and interest of 1 percent a month begins. Under KRS 134.420 the lien may last 11 years under any owner.

The county attorney sends two notices, one within 30 days of the transfer and one within 60. The Clerk then sets a sale 90 to 135 days out, and a certificate buyer may add substantial fees. Request a payoff from the Sheriff before April 15 and from the Clerk after it. Have the closing agent pay it from proceeds.

Ask for the payoff in writing and check that it covers every year with a balance, not only the latest bill.

sections.h2: Selling a house in Meade County
sections.html:
Meade County was created in 1823 and covers 325 square miles. The Ohio River forms its 56-mile northern line, facing Indiana. Karst terrain with sinkholes covers much of the land, and the northwest sits on a plateau behind the Dripping Springs Escarpment. Brandenburg is the seat, Ekron and Muldraugh are the other cities, and Doe Valley and Fort Knox are census-designated places. Meade lies in the Louisville metro area, within reach of the job centers at Elizabethtown and Fort Knox, and workers travel a mean 33.0 minutes to their jobs.

Meade County Schools, with Meade County High School, teach most children, while families living on the Fort Knox base are zoned to the Defense Department's schools. The county keeps Eastern time.

Sinkholes are common in this terrain, and a house with one, or with deferred repairs, can stall a conventional sale. Ground conditions vary from one parcel to the next, so a buyer's inspection may ask about them. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can close without those fixes.

Start by phoning the PVA to confirm the parcel record and any homestead claim, then ask the Sheriff for the current bill. If the sale will close after April 15, plan to get the payoff from the County Clerk instead. Expect the title company to ask for both figures, along with a copy of the deed. When the owner has died, bring the papers showing who may sign the deed.

Showings go better when the house is ready for a walk-through, but you aren't required to fix anything for a cash sale. If the sinkhole question comes up, a buyer will want to know what you know about it, so be ready to answer plainly. Keep copies of your tax receipts for recent years. They show the title company the bills were paid and speed up the payoff check. If a tenant lives in the house, tell the buyer early and give the lease terms, since a lease may stay in force after the sale. Finally, ask the Sheriff about payment methods for your closing date, because the personal-check rule near the end of the season can matter if the closing falls close to April 15

faqs.q: Where do I pay the Meade County Sheriff?
faqs.a: Go to 516 Hillcrest Drive, Suite 14, in Brandenburg, or call (270) 422-4937. Suite 3, the PVA, can't accept payments.

faqs.q: When does the Meade County Sheriff stop taking personal checks?
faqs.a: From two weeks before April 15 onward. Cash, cards, money orders and cashier's checks are still accepted.

faqs.q: When is the homestead filing cutoff in Meade County?
faqs.a: The PVA sets a spring date each year for a place on the November bill. Call the office for the current cutoff.

faqs.q: What is the state rate in Meade County?
faqs.a: The state's 2025 rate is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value. County, school and district levies come on top.

faqs.q: What becomes of Meade County bills left open after April 15?
faqs.a: The Clerk receives them as certificates of delinquency and files a lien. Interest accrues at 1 percent monthly, and the Clerk may schedule a sale within 90 to 135 days.
